content: The World Health Organization (WHO) defines palliative care as the prevention and relief of suffering for patients, including children, and their families who are facing challenges associated with life-threatening illnesses. This care addresses physical, psychological, social, and spiritual suffering in patients, as well as the psychological, social, and spiritual distress experienced by family members. Palliative care involves early identification, thorough assessment, and treatment of these issues to enhance quality of life, promote dignity and comfort, and potentially influence the course of illness positively. It provides support to patients and families throughout the illness trajectory and integrates with prevention, early diagnosis, and treatment of serious or life-limiting health conditions. Palliative care is applicable early in the course of illness alongside therapies aimed at prolonging life. It also serves as an alternative to disease-modifying or life-sustaining treatments of questionable value near the end of life. This care is relevant for individuals living with long-term physical, psychological, social, or spiritual consequences of serious illnesses or their treatments. It also supports bereaved family members after a patient’s death and seeks to mitigate the harmful effects of poverty on patients and families, protecting them from financial hardship due to illness or disability. Importantly, palliative care does not hasten death but focuses on achieving adequate comfort for the patient in alignment with their values. Palliative care should be accessible at all levels of healthcare systems, including in patients’ homes, and should be delivered by healthcare workers with varying levels of training, from basic to specialist. It encourages active involvement by communities and community members, improves continuity of care, strengthens healthcare systems, and promotes universal health coverage (UHC). The specific types and severity of suffering vary based on geopolitical, socioeconomic, and cultural factors. Children and their families in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) often endure unhealthy social conditions and have less access to disease prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and specialized services compared to those in high-income countries (HICs). For example, many children in LMICs lack access to cancer chemotherapy, radiation therapy, oncologic surgery, effective treatment for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, or neonatal and pediatric intensive care. Palliative care should not replace disease prevention and treatment or critical care but should complement these services. Palliative care workers have a responsibility to advocate for these services where they are not yet accessible. Pediatric palliative care (PPC) is particularly important, as children under 20 years of age make up 35% of the global population and 40% in the least-developed nations. Each year, up to 21 million children may require PPC, with 5 million dying annually while experiencing serious health-related suffering. Over 98% of these children are in LMICs. Despite this need, PPC is not prioritized globally, and access to these services is extremely limited in many countries. For instance, in sub-Saharan Africa, less than 1% of children needing PPC in Kenya have access to it, and less than 5% in South Africa and Zimbabwe. PPC differs from adult palliative care in several ways. Children undergo continuous physical, developmental, and psychosocial changes as they grow, requiring providers to assess and respond to their unique developmental stages and needs. Communication with children and their families must be sensitive to the child’s developmental stage, language, culture, and understanding of illness. PPC also considers the child’s values and seeks their input on treatment and care goals whenever possible. Children’s dependence on adults varies widely, from the total dependence of neonates to the relative independence of adolescents. Serious or life-threatening illnesses in children profoundly impact families, often leading to financial hardship, emotional distress, and strained family dynamics. PPC must address these challenges with social supports and family-centered care. The types of health conditions requiring PPC are diverse, including advanced chronic non-communicable diseases, HIV/AIDS, severe prematurity, birth trauma, congenital anomalies, severe disabilities, and injuries. Many pediatric conditions are rare and not seen in adults, making diagnosis and prognosis challenging. PPC also involves creating child-friendly clinical environments that promote comfort and well-being. This includes allowing family members to be present, providing soothing surroundings, and offering age-appropriate distractions and comforts. PPC aims to improve the quality of life for children and their families, strengthen healthcare systems, and implement cost-effective service models, contributing to the goal of UHC.
